title: The Calm Before the Storm- AI Risk, and Market Fragility - Systematic Investor - Ep.357

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/The Calm Before the Storm- AI Risk, and Market Fragility - Systematic Investor - Ep.357.docx

speakers: Jim (guest; options/volatility strategist, surname garbled in captions)
summary: July 2025 free-flowing macro and options-flow discussion. Argues vol compression plus doubled hedge-fund positioning and expiration cycles make markets fragile; a structural inflation, debt-monetization and steepener thesis; AI unemployment; scenario forecast of a mild decline then relief, with year-end magnification.

coverage.note: banter; hedge fund and structured product growth; fast recovery
call-driven VIX spike; Belt and Road
rare earths, AI beneficiaries, broker concentration
trend update and CTA numbers; gold call question
gold calls, oil puts, equity vol and rotation
momentum-value, concentrated commodities, FX and bond vol
bond vol, debt jubilee, vol compression and positioning
dispersion, momentum-value indicator, hedge fund pain
inflation to employment, CPI vs PPI, BLS estimates
libertarianism, Doge, deregulation; transition to market outlook

completeness_estimate: 0.78 - the first reader captured nearly all of the main arguments and forecasts; it missed some supporting data (index returns, equity flatness since 2021, copper move), data-integrity mechanisms and the PTJ allocation debate details.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: the investment size and hedge funds has grown dramatically as well as uh the structure product and those two things are starting to interact.
claims.claim: Hedge fund assets and structured-product issuance have both grown dramatically and now interact, so positioning is very different from the past and market dynamics are changing.
claims.indicator: hedge fund size and structured-product issuance
claims.testable: partly - hedge fund asset and issuance data

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the recovery has been the quickest uh that we've ever seen. I think 57 days from a 20% draw down or more
claims.claim: The spring 2025 equity recovery from a 20% drawdown took 57 days, the fastest on record and without Fed easing.
claims.indicator: S&P 500 recovery time from a 20% drawdown

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: massive call v call call buying into that decline and in the S&P 500 specifically
claims.claim: The April 2025 VIX spike was driven by massive S&P 500 call buying (a call squeeze), not put demand or skew, unlike August 2024; attribution matters when comparing similar VIX levels.
claims.indicator: VIX decomposition into call vs put and skew

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: if you try and bully people around and and uh you know push push them in a corner um uh they're going to look for alternatives
claims.claim: Pressure on trade partners pushes them to alternatives, and China's record Belt and Road activity shows it positioning as the stable partner, making resources a long-run theme.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: who the benefits of AI acrue to uh have not been made clear yet. Um, and we have been talking about uh for some time that it's likely actually to to go to uh resources
claims.claim: The benefits of AI may accrue to resources because of the power and materials required; hence big tech buying nuclear power and rare earth stakes (Apple $0.5B; US DoD).
claims.testable: partly - capex and commodity demand data

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it is now the top three among the top three brokers of 125 of the world's 150 50 biggest stock trading clients and I'm thinking wow that's a big concentration risk.
claims.claim: Goldman Sachs is a top-three prime broker for 125 of the 150 largest trading clients, up from about 80 relationships, so concentration among a few brokers is a systemic risk in a crisis.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: big companies are getting bigger um and uh you know happens in technology like the Mac 7 right
claims.claim: Rising concentration in tech (Mag 7) and finance gives size benefits but increases fragility because firms cannot pivot when something goes wrong.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: My own trend barometer actually reflects this perfectly. It's it stands at 45 which is completely neutral.
claims.claim: July 2025 trend followers were flat: long copper and equities, short US fixed income while long European bonds; Beta 50 -0.13% in July, -3.38% YTD; SG CTA -7.59% YTD.
claims.direction: long metals and equities, short US bonds

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: if you go into these populist periods 60s7s we've talked about right these kind of these periods where um you uh you get inflation uh and it's structural
claims.claim: In structural inflation or populist periods (1960s-70s) gold is the best-performing asset and is also the most volatile, so long-dated gold calls win in both price and implied volatility.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: we said go sell puts in oil. Uh both assets tend to be very bullish in these periods. um but very different in how they are bullish.
claims.claim: In these periods oil rises steadily with a floor from geopolitical conflict while trade falls under protectionism, so selling oil puts is favored whereas gold calls suit gold's volatile rise.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: the things that work best, the volatility that works best is actually not equity vault, which is the first thing that people think about.
claims.claim: In inflationary periods nominal equity indices go nowhere, so equity index volatility is a poor hedge and the opportunity lies in rotation and dispersion (e.g. growth vs value) under the surface.
claims.direction: avoid long index vol; trade dispersion

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: momentum versus value breakdown in that's significant. We saw this last summer.
claims.claim: A breakdown in momentum versus value, which also occurred in summer 2024, is a key tell of hedge fund positioning pain; cross-factor options plays offer big payoffs.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: most of the uranium in the world comes from just a couple countries Kazakhstan being the biggest Canada being the other
claims.claim: Assets whose supply is concentrated (uranium: Kazakhstan, Canada; copper: Chile; rare earths) become unstable and convex in geopolitical conflict because a supplier can flex its muscle.
claims.direction: long uranium, copper, rare earths convexity

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: FX is going to be the best play in V for the decade.
claims.claim: FX volatility is the best volatility play for the decade because gold is more of a currency than a commodity and currency instability will rise; bond volatility is the next best.
claims.direction: long FX vol and bond vol

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: if you don't see the similar similarities between Nixon and Arthur Burns, I can't help you.
claims.claim: Political pressure on the Fed (Powell as with Nixon and Burns) is expected to bring dramatic bond moves, a steepener, a 'debt jubilee' within 5-10 years and cross-country currency volatility (yen-dollar carry blowup last August).

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: there is a historic uh amount of uh v compression happening um which is tied to these massive inflows as we've talked about before from into structured products
claims.claim: Structured-product inflows plus low summer volume compress implied and realised volatility at the index level; paired with doubled hedge fund gross leverage this creates positioning the market is not used to.
claims.testable: yes - issuance and implied vol data

correction.issue: Slight misreading of the number: Jim said hedge fund positioning (size) has doubled in four to five years, while gross leverage in long/short equity is typically about 3x; he did not say gross leverage doubled.
correction.fix: Structured-product inflows plus low summer volume compress implied and realised volatility at the index level; hedge fund positioning (assets/exposure) has doubled in four to five years with long/short equity gross leverage near 3x.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: If you have massive V compression, no volume, and you have long short equity positioning, that's gross, that's massive.
claims.claim: Index-level volatility compression forces individual stocks away from each other (high dispersion), so crowded long/short equity funds with large gross leverage suffer pain in low-volume summers.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: Momentum value versus value often leads the market lower. It's a leading indicator.
claims.claim: A rollover in the momentum-minus-value spread leads the equity market lower (summer 2024 into July expiration); it is a good tell for hedge fund pain.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: if you go look at the last two years and look at kind of expirations. I mean we've talked about it for years.
claims.claim: Options expirations (especially quarter-end and the August/September cycle) are becoming major turning points for the S&P because of huge options volumes.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: a tariff is a tax obviously and that tax gets borne by who? First corporations eventually people but first corporations.
claims.claim: Tariff costs hit corporate margins first, then prices; earnings and guidance show it before CPI, so watch margin compression, then inflation, then employment.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: CPI includes imports. PPI do not it does not include imports.
claims.claim: CPI includes imports while PPI does not, so a CPI-PPI divergence is informative while tariffs apply.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the portion that essentially is an estimate uh has gone up from 9% of the number uh to 35% of the CPI in June was based on estimates
claims.claim: The share of CPI based on estimates rose from 9% to 35% by June 2025, so official data may be less objective.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: we're going to have to start taking the government numbers with with a greater great you know grain assault um and and uh you know start looking a little bit more at the private numbers
claims.claim: Official payrolls diverged from ADP (job losses) with government jobs filling the gap, so private data sources deserve more weight than government data.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: the best outcome for Trump is not to fire Powell, but just to make it believable that he could do it at any moment.
claims.claim: A credible threat to fire Powell (steepener: front down, back up) is more useful than acting, because firing would raise long yields and the board still votes on rates; markets reacted at once to the letter news.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: a cyclical slowdown. Um that's a and b you probably want kind of markets a little bit lower as well.
claims.claim: To get rate cuts before the midterms, the administration needs a slowdown and lower markets (a controlled demolition), so a market decline may be tolerated.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: in Trump's first period, he kind of normalized 4% deficits. That was kind of suddenly fine. uh now he's kind of doing the same with six to 7% uh deficits.
claims.claim: Paul Tudor Jones argues markets will eventually force debt stabilization, with lower bonds, dollar and equities; normalizing 6%+ deficits drags equity returns and calls for negative real rates (fed funds 2-2.5% against 3-3.5% inflation).

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: the steepener will could move even faster now because before
claims.claim: The curve steepener was easy while inflation hedges were cheap; now that inflation hedging is hard and expensive, long-end repricing is more likely to move fast.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: as long as we're the reserve currency, you know, the US's dollar is the reserve currency of the world. Um yeah, that the debt can be monetized.
claims.claim: The US will eventually monetize debt (like Japan, where debt is mostly domestic) as dollar primacy persists; this implies negative rates, a front-end cut leading to a massive steepener, then Twist-like operations.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: I could borrow money at let's say 4% and inflation is 6% or whatever what is everybody with any money going to do?
claims.claim: Holding long-term rates below inflation causes borrowing to buy real assets and pull forward demand, an inflation spiral as in the 1970s.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: the place you're starting to see it are the 30-year bonds particularly in Japan
claims.claim: Long-dated bonds (30-year JGB, Bund at 14-year highs) show stress first because the back end cannot be controlled.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: the S&P 500 uh during that 14-year period, that inflationary period lost uh you know, about 50% or you know, or so of its value
claims.claim: In the 1968-82 inflationary period the S&P lost about half its value in real terms; equities are not an inflation hedge because rates drive the discount rate.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: if you can go get a 20-year bond or 10-year bond for 20% why the hell would you ever buy uh the S&P for anything less?
claims.claim: Earnings yield tracks the 10-year yield over multi-year horizons (1968: 4.5% yield with a 22x P/E; 1982: 20% yield with a 4.5x P/E), so rising long yields compress multiples.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: There are some equities that you got to be very tactical that will expand profit margins right into uh increasing interest rates and that's a sub a small subset about 20 to 25% of the S&P 500.
claims.claim: Only about 20-25% of S&P companies can expand margins into rising rates; the rest face both multiple and margin contraction.
claims.direction: select firms with negative working capital

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: we think 30 to 50% of a portfolio should be non-correlated
claims.claim: Hold 30-50% of the portfolio in non-correlated strategies rather than just assets, as in 1960s-style investing.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: The unemployment rate for college graduates this last year is at 9% in the United States.
claims.claim: College-graduate unemployment of about 9% (versus 4% overall, and 6-6.5% a year ago) is a leading indicator of rising unemployment, concentrated in computer science and similar AI-exposed fields.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: UBI is coming by the way.
claims.claim: AI job losses plus populism lead to universal basic income, more fiscal spending and more protectionism, a volatile political and fiscal cycle by the next election.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: the Doge movement of really hollowing out uh regulatory authority um is going to give more
claims.claim: Cuts to regulators are said to enable data control and favor wealthy corporations.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: until positioning gets back on sides that it's hard for uh markets to go down.
claims.claim: Institutional short positioning must be covered before a meaningful decline, so while hedge funds and institutions are short, the market grinds up with supportive vanna/charm flows from volatility supply.
claims.indicator: institutional short positioning, vanna and charm flows
claims.direction: long-biased drift while shorts are covered

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: The end of the year is a bit of a magnifier to whatever is happening going into the end of the year.
claims.claim: Year-end rebalancing and releveraging magnify whatever trend is in place going in, so a decline or rally continues into year end.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: the best outcome is a slow boil the frog kind of you know heat up the water
claims.claim: A slow, low-volatility drift lower (not a sharp spike) is the likely path; buying puts in advance is poor because a real decline needs hedges to fail and volatility to stay low.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: it's likely to be a small 1-mon decline, I think 2 1/2 to 5%.
claims.claim: Forecast: a 2.5-5% decline into July/August opex, then possibly a further 5-12% drop (10-15% total, back to about 5700), with a relief rally of 10-15% around September opex.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: this is more of a 2022 type decline
claims.claim: If the decline is not scary, retail keeps buying and hedges fail, producing a painful grind lower like 2022 and 2018 rather than a V bottom.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: unless we start getting a decline now, like soon.
claims.claim: If no decline occurs within 1.5-2 months, the setup shifts toward a 1998-style blow-off top into the midterms, resolving badly after them.
claims.direction: long equities then reduce after midterms

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: knowing that those are your more most likely paths itself is incredibly valuable because you can bet on both paths um at the same time.
claims.claim: Knowing two plausible scenarios lets the trader position for both (options) rather than commit to one forecast.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Sockchen trend down 21 basis points down 10.18 this year.
claims.claim: Mid-July 2025 CTA indices were deeply negative year to date (SG Trend -10.18%, SG CTA -7.59%, Short Term Traders -4.61%, Beta 50 -3.38%) while MSCI World was +10.1% and the S&P 500 +7.25%, so trend followers lagged badly after the April whipsaw; the S&P aggregate bond index was +3% YTD.
claims.indicator: SG Trend, SG CTA, SG Short Term Traders, BTOP50, MSCI World, S&P 500
claims.direction: trend lags equities after V-shaped reversal

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: 2021 at the peak in 2021, we're only up 25% or so in uh four years, right? Or three and a half years. Uh and at the lows, by the way, just in April, we were unchanged.
claims.claim: Nominal equity returns since the 2021 peak are only about +25% and were flat at the April 2025 lows, supporting the claim that equity indices go nowhere in a structurally inflationary decade.
claims.direction: equity index sideways in nominal terms

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: Drunk Miller being one of them has made a ton of money on Russell calls versus at two times now speculating that that he's doing it again here
claims.claim: Large traders such as Druckenmiller have profited from Russell 2000 call buying twice and a big buyer of Russell calls is showing again, read by Jim as a positioning play squeezing short hedge funds and value/small-cap laggards.
claims.conditions: Works when the shorts are crowded.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: copper actually is also sure biggest one day move since 1968 uh only a couple of weeks ago and copper production is very concentrated in Chile
claims.claim: Copper's record one-day move (since 1968) after tariff news, with production concentrated in Chile, shows how concentrated-supply commodities become convex and unstable when policy changes.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: I don't think there's any reason to to do anything uh less than a year. Um because this could take several years.
claims.claim: Long-volatility bets on the inflation/bond thesis should be at least a year out, because the thesis could take several years to play out and timing is uncertain.
claims.conditions: Thesis is structural, not a near-term call.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: gross leverage and long short equity uh at hedge funds is usually 3x sometimes bigger.
claims.claim: Long/short equity is 40-50% of hedge fund assets, runs about 3x gross leverage, and total hedge fund positioning has doubled in four to five years, creating a behemoth, crowded exposure that is vulnerable in low-volume summers.
claims.indicator: hedge fund gross leverage; long/short equity share of HF assets
claims.conditions: Low summer volume and vol compression.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: coming from the same pods that then go off and start their own and um so there's also kind of a similar set of you know factor models that everybody uses
claims.claim: Hedge fund staff come from the same pods and use similar factor models, so positioning is correlated even when each fund tries to avoid crowded trades.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: Hedge funds were actually equal weight if not more. Now they're getting now they're short and the the pain trade is getting hit
claims.claim: Unlike summer 2024, when hedge funds were not short, in 2025 hedge funds and institutions are net short, so the pain trade hits the short side and the summer becomes a degrossing event in an illiquid market.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: Part of what happened last summer is that hedge fund pain eventually led to a degen carry trade kicked in um kind of exacerbated the move.
claims.claim: In 2024 hedge fund pain was amplified by the yen carry-trade unwind; Jim does not expect that second leg this time.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: This is a quarter with pretty soft tariffs, right? Because a lot of it was rolled back and so we haven't even seen the worst to come.
claims.claim: Q2 earnings reflect only soft tariffs because many were rolled back; the full margin and inflation effect has not yet shown, so guidance is the key release.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: revisions happening happening on the employment side that were dramatic and consistent um that made all the employment numbers look great
claims.claim: Jim says that during the previous four years employment data were revised repeatedly in the same direction, flattering initial prints and fixed afterwards, so the first release is biased.
claims.conditions: Claim is the speaker's, no figures given.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: the Fed is data dependent and these are the data a lot of the data that they look at, it makes sense, right, that the that an administration would want those numbers to look a certain way
claims.claim: Because the Fed is data-dependent, an administration that wants rate cuts has an incentive to shape the macro data (CPI, payrolls), so official releases deserve extra scepticism while Powell is under pressure.
claims.conditions: Speculative, Jim says 'where there's smoke, there's fire'.
claims.testable: partly - data quality can be audited

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: they've removed actually resources from the BLS um uh and and said,
claims.claim: Cutting BLS resources forced more reliance on estimates (historically 10% or lower, now 30-35% of CPI), turning the data into a qualitative judgement made by appointees.
claims.indicator: share of CPI based on estimates
claims.testable: yes - share of imputed prices is published

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there are cost overruns on the construction or refurbishment of the Federal Reserve. And of course, the only way to remove him would be for quote unquote cause.
claims.claim: The shift to citing Federal Reserve renovation cost overruns is read as building a 'cause' to remove Powell, which would otherwise require cause.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: this is essentially like a shadow Fed move where you're moving in and you're projecting policy without actually doing anything.
claims.claim: A credible but unexecuted threat to remove Powell acts as a shadow-Fed move: markets price in easier policy at once, supporting equities and controlling the narrative while hedge funds are short.
claims.conditions: Fails if the threat is actually executed (long yields rise).

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: He felt that on a volad adjusted basis gold, Bitcoin and equities uh would be uh where he would um where he would invest kind of thing.
claims.claim: Paul Tudor Jones's reported ideal portfolio on a volatility-adjusted basis is gold, Bitcoin and equities, while his highest conviction is the curve steepener; Niels says he does not agree.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: if you think the US is going to go into some austerity um and and and government officials uh are going to stop spending um uh I got some beachfront property to sell you in Arizona.
claims.claim: Fiscal austerity is not credible, so spending and debt keep rising until the Fed must monetise the debt; this underlies the steepener and inflation thesis.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: essentially it's going to be a soft default basically um uh you're better off they're better off doing it all at once
claims.claim: Debt monetisation amounts to a soft default; it would be better done at once but political unpalatability makes a gradual front-end cut then curve-control path more likely, which steepens the curve.
claims.direction: front end down, long end up

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's this idea that you know what you're watching isn't real, but we're still watching it.
claims.claim: Markets can tolerate an obviously unsustainable situation (debt, bond market) for a long time until a trigger makes it undeniable (Emperor's new clothes, Biden debate), so timing is the hard part.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: inflation inflation is uh may seem subdued now. Um it it hasn't gone away for a while and we've talked about why it is not going away for good.
claims.claim: Inflation is only apparently subdued; it should normalise at a higher level and become a serious problem within 5 to 10 years, earlier than most expect.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: you can lose 50 75% in both those assets um in a matter of uh months, year, a year.
claims.claim: Even if gold and Bitcoin suit a structural inflationary period, a concentrated vol-adjusted allocation risks 50 to 75% drawdowns in months, which is a poor risk-reward compared with non-correlated strategies.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: you want to be focused on on the companies that have negative working capital and and are uh have improving uh outcomes on the equity side
claims.claim: Within equities in a rising-rate regime, prefer companies with negative working capital and improving results, the ones that can expand margins while multiples compress.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: if you're really worried about high interest rates, is gold really going to help you with that?
claims.claim: Niels questions the PTJ portfolio: gold and Bitcoin are not natural hedges against high interest rates, though they could rise if the whole system blows up or on crypto support.
claims.conditions: Regime dependent: rates shock vs system shock.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: he's saying that he could see 10 to 20% unemployment in 1 to 5 years due to AI which is white collar jobs uh specifically
claims.claim: Dario Amodei's reported forecast is 10 to 20% unemployment in 1 to 5 years from AI, concentrated in white-collar jobs; Jim thinks this is likely and a big deal.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: those hires are now doing the work of three hires.
claims.claim: Anecdotal evidence of AI productivity: new hires do the work of three or four, so hiring stops sooner and faster than expected.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: AI started to thrive um in a in a period when you know it was 1982 okay well you know free market economics
claims.claim: The same AI shock is manageable in a free-market, supply-side cycle like 1982 but is volatile in the present populist, unequal, concentrated-power cycle, so political regime conditions the macro outcome.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: that libertarianism is as big a threat to the US as socialism
claims.claim: Paul Tudor Jones reportedly sees libertarianism, i.e. no safeguards on AI, as as big a threat as socialism, which Niels links to AI regulation moratoria.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the fourth turning and we still have a few years left of that.
claims.claim: The Strauss-Howe 'fourth turning' generational cycle is used as a frame for a crisis-era with several years remaining, consistent with populism and fiscal expansion.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: we're also starting to see sentiment percolating to kind of record levels.
claims.claim: Bullish sentiment is near record while institutions are short, a setup where positioning fuel for higher prices builds and then runs out.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: Doesn't mean the weighing machine won't take over. Uh the weighing machine will take over.
claims.claim: Flow-driven grinds (vol supply, short covering) are temporary; fundamentals ('weighing machine') eventually dominate.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: there is a big dislocation between August skew and September skew and that's kind of a clue that there's a lot of pain sitting out there in that quarterly potential pain
claims.claim: A large gap between August and September S&P skew signals pain concentrated at the September quarterly expiry; front puts decaying while back skew stays high could force a chase and a grind lower with vol compression.
claims.indicator: S&P skew term structure August vs September

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: the pain will probably still uh continue momentum versus value until about you know middle of a uh sorry late August or so
claims.claim: Momentum-versus-value pain is expected to last until late August, then turn as volatility is released from its floor.
claims.direction: momentum down, value up until late August

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: The next two months are basically uh you know all the things we've been waiting for are coming now. It's earnings, it's inflation, it's employment and all the things.
claims.claim: The decisive data (earnings, inflation, employment, Powell/Trump outcome) arrive within two months and decide how the relief rally resolves.

claims.speaker: Jim (guest, options/volatility strategist)
claims.quote: support it along the way as well, which will also help create compression, yeah, control demolition, which I think they probably wouldn't mind.
claims.claim: Authorities are expected to cushion any decline, which compresses volatility and makes the decline a slow, controlled one.

claims.quote: you have a midterm coming next year and then you have them taking on the Fed chairmanship in in in June, right, next year.
